In my internship last year I was put in charge of three other interns, which mostly meant I noticed things before anyone else did.
Chandrika had written her own file reader for the sales data. It took her ten days. Every time a file had a comma inside a name, it broke. There was a standard library that handled all of that in one line.
When I brought it up, Chandrika went pink and said, "Mine is almost there." She'd open her code and walk me through it with real affection, like a thing she'd raised. I realised she wasn't defending the code, she was defending those ten days.
So I asked Mr Pillai, our mentor, to set aside a Friday demo where Chandrika showed what she'd learned building it. Then we switched to the library. She even suggested it herself.

qa.a: It took her ten days.

qa.a: The narrator felt understanding and a little sympathetic, realising that Chandrika was defending the ten days of effort, not the code's quality.

qa.a: It honoured Chandrika's learning and effort in public, so dropping the code no longer felt like losing those ten days.

qa.a: She may have felt relieved and respected, able to let go once her work had been seen.

Studio mentor's note, Thursday. From Kalyani, lead designer.
Himani has spent four months hand-drawing every icon for the café client's menu. Today, the client asked for a version that works on the delivery app, and the hand-drawn set doesn't scale.
I watched her go through it. She didn't argue. She sat with the files and said out loud, "If I were starting fresh today, knowing it needs to scale, would I draw these by hand?" After a long pause: "No. I'd use a vector set and customise it."
Then she added, "But I'm framing six of the originals for the café wall. They're still the best thing I've made."
What I did next: I approved the switch, gave her two days for it, and asked the client about the framed set. They loved it.

qa.a: She probably felt torn, proud of four months of work but aware it might not suit what the client now needed.

Tuesday night
Two years on this bookshelf app and today I finally asked myself the question Farhan asked me last month: "If you were starting today, would you build it this way?"
Honest answer: no. Half the code is from when I didn't know what I was doing. There are free tools now that do the sorting better. I've been keeping it because of all the late nights, not because it's good.
That stings a bit. I'm proud of those nights.
So here's the plan. I'll move my own library to one of the free tools this weekend. But I'm keeping the old app's code, printing the first screen I ever made, and pinning it above my desk.
Amandeep, you built something. It's allowed to be finished.

qa.a: Amandeep had worked on it for two years.

qa.a: Amandeep feels a sting of loss mixed with pride in the late nights, but also clear-headed about moving on.

qa.q: What could others take from Amandeep's plan?
qa.a: You can switch to a better tool for daily use while still honouring your work, like printing the first screen and keeping the code.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel reading this entry?
qa.a: Farhan might feel glad and a little proud that the question helped Amandeep make a calm decision.

When I was nine, beta, in our old house in Bhuj, my cousin Bhavna and I were doing a jigsaw of a peacock. Five hundred pieces. We had finished everything except the tail when my mother called me to the market.
All the way there and back I kept seeing that tail. Which blue piece went where? I bumped into a cow, I was so lost in it. My mother laughed at me.
My homework was finished that morning. I couldn't have told you one sum from it. But that tail, I remembered every gap.
I ran straight back, and Bhavna had waited. "Hansa, I didn't touch it," she said. We finished it together before dinner. Your Dadi has never forgotten that peacock.

qa.a: It was a jigsaw of a peacock.

qa.q: Why did young Hansa keep thinking about the tail at the market?
qa.a: She felt restless and a bit puzzled, because the unfinished tail stayed open in her mind while the finished homework slipped away.

qa.q: What was the choice inside the story that helped Hansa settle the nagging feeling?
qa.a: Rushing straight back and finishing the tail with Bhavna closed the open task, so her mind could rest.

qa.a: Bhavna probably felt loyal and a little impatient, wanting to finish it together and pleased when Hansa came running back.

grounding: A child called away mid-jigsaw keeps thinking about the unfinished part and rushes back, while her finished homework slips from mind.

Deepak had just four pieces left in the train jigsaw when the power went off and his sister Gopika called, "Come, we have to leave for Mama's wedding now!"
In the car, in the rain, Deepak couldn't stop thinking. The red engine piece. The corner with the smoke. Where did the last blue one go?
At the wedding, Gopika asked what he had eaten for breakfast. He didn't remember. He'd also finished his maths worksheet that morning and couldn't recall a single question. But he could picture every gap in the puzzle.
They got home late. The power was still off. Deepak took a torch, knelt on the floor and pressed the last four pieces in. Only then did he yawn.

qa.q: How many pieces did Deepak have left when the power went off?
qa.a: He had just four pieces left.

qa.q: How can you tell the unfinished jigsaw was on Deepak's mind?
qa.a: He felt restless and couldn't stop picturing the gaps, even at the wedding, and only relaxed enough to yawn once it was done.

qa.q: What could Deepak try next time he has to stop a puzzle suddenly?
qa.a: He could jot a quick note of what's left, like which pieces go where, so his mind can let it go until he returns.

qa.q: What is it like for Gopika to be with Deepak at the wedding?
qa.a: Gopika might find him distracted and a bit funny, since he can't remember breakfast but keeps thinking about a puzzle.

grounding: A child pulled away from a nearly finished jigsaw keeps thinking about it, forgets finished tasks and finishes it by torchlight.

On Sunday mornings Jaya did the newspaper word search in the flat's living room. She had found seven of the ten words when her cousin Devika called, "Jaya, come, we're late for the dentist!"
In the auto, Jaya muttered, "Pomegranate. Where's pomegranate?"
"You're still on that?" Devika laughed.
At the clinic, Devika asked what books Jaya had finished that week. Jaya frowned. She'd finished two, but couldn't remember the second one's name. Pomegranate, though. And the two words after it.
As soon as they got home, Jaya ran to the table, grabbed the pencil and circled the last three words. She let out a huge breath and flopped on the sofa, happy.

qa.a: She had found seven of the ten words.

qa.a: She felt relieved and happy, because the unfinished word search had been tugging at her mind all morning.

"Just one more," she whispered. Her physics test was at nine.
